# Intel ISA and SIMD reading notes for Sapphire Rapids / Xeon Platinum 8454H

The source comparisons below describe the implementation before the 2026-10-13 SIMD/AMX optimization. The current implementation and measurements are documented in [8454H_PERFORMANCE_BASELINE.md](../../../docs/8454H_PERFORMANCE_BASELINE.md).

Retrieved 2026-10-13. Official PDFs, their hashes, version/date metadata, final download URLs, page counts, and rights notes are recorded in [`../manuals/manifest.json`](../manuals/manifest.json). This is a selected reading set, not a mirror of all ten SDM volumes and not a claim that every page was read.

## Collected references and extraction

- Current SDM Version 093: Volume 1 (Basic Architecture), Volume 2B (instruction reference M–U), and Volume 2C (V). Official index: [Intel SDM page](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html). Text was extracted with Ghostscript `txtwrite` to `/tmp/intel-manuals-extract/sdm-vol1-v093.txt`, `sdm-vol2b-v093.txt`, and `sdm-vol2c-v093.txt`. Ghostscript reports 600, 771, and 782 pages respectively.
- Intel Optimization Reference Manual Volume 1, document 248966-050US, April 2024. It was selected because its Chapter 20 directly covers Sapphire Rapids AMX and includes programming examples. Text was extracted to `/tmp/intel-manuals-extract/optimization-reference-manual-v1-050.txt` (895 pages). Ghostscript emitted repeated `Subtype of a TT CID font is not /CIDFontType2` warnings during extraction; the full 2.8 MB text file was produced, and key findings were checked against the PDF's page headings and SDM instruction pseudocode. Treat extraction of unusual glyphs/tables cautiously.
- The official [Intel Intrinsics Guide](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html) was saved as `intrinsics-guide.html`, and the official offline download linked from that page as `intrinsics-guide-offline.zip`. Release notes in the bundle say version 3.6.9, dated 2024-07-12. The expanded bundle is in `intrinsics-guide-offline/`; it carries instruction/intrinsic metadata in `Intel Intrinsics Guide/files/data.js` and performance metadata in `perf2.js`. This is useful for discovery and intrinsic names, but it is older than SDM v093 and should not override the SDM's current architectural pseudocode.

## High-value sections for this project

Line numbers below refer to the Ghostscript text extracts in `/tmp/intel-manuals-extract/`; the printed page numbers are also given so they can be checked against the PDFs.

| Topic | Primary source location | What the source states |
|---|---|---|
| Sapphire Rapids / Golden Cove | Optimization Manual v1-050 §2.2, printed pp. 2-5–2-6; extract lines 2486–2510 | Sapphire Rapids processors use Golden Cove cores and add AMX and AVX-512; 4th Gen Xeon Scalable details follow. This is architecture guidance, not per-SKU enumeration. |
| AMX tile computation and BF16 numerical behavior | SDM Vol. 2B, `TDPBF16PS`, printed pp. 4-715–4-716; extract lines 28329–28382 | BF16 pairs are packed in dwords; each corresponding pair is multiplied and accumulated to FP32. Per the instruction description, accumulation is RNE; input denormals are treated as zero; output denormals are flushed to zero; MXCSR is not consulted or updated. The pseudocode makes the pair products and final pairwise sum explicit. |
| BF16 convert lane order | SDM Vol. 2C, `VCVTNE2PS2BF16`, printed pp. 5-32–5-33; extract lines 1303–1361 | For output word index `i < KL/2`, the converted value comes from `src2`; for `i >= KL/2`, it comes from `src1[i-KL/2]`. Therefore the lower half of BF16 output lanes comes from the third operand (`src2`), and the upper half comes from the second operand (`src1`). |
| FP32-to-BF16 convert semantics | SDM Vol. 2C, `VCVTNEPS2BF16`, printed pp. 5-38–5-39; extract lines 1504–1594 | RNE is fixed; MXCSR is ignored; input denormals are treated as zero and output denormals are flushed. Pseudocode gives signed zero for zero/denormal inputs, a distinct infinity path, a NaN path, and for normal inputs the `0x7fff + LSB` rounding bias before taking the upper 16 bits. |
| MXCSR FTZ, DAZ, rounding | SDM Vol. 1 §§10.2.3.2–10.2.3.4, printed pp. 10-4–10-5; extract lines 11387–11424 | MXCSR RC controls SIMD FP rounding; FTZ flushes masked underflow results to signed zero; DAZ converts denormal source operands to signed zero. The manual says both FTZ and DAZ modes are not IEEE 754 compatible. BF16-specific instructions above independently define their own behavior and do not consult MXCSR. |
| BF16 numerical format | SDM Vol. 1 §§4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2, printed pp. 4-6–4-7; extract lines 4585–4616 | BF16 is sign+8-bit exponent+7-bit fraction; the manual distinguishes its numerical range from FP16 and says BF16 computations use RNE, replace BF16 input denormals by zero, flush FP32 underflow results to zero, and neither read/update MXCSR nor raise FP exceptions. |
| Runtime feature enumeration | SDM Vol. 1 CPUID tables, printed pp. 21-29 and 21-31; extract around lines 20230–20355 | AMX_TILE, AMX_BF16, AMX_INT8, AVX512_FP16, AVX512_BF16, and AMX_FP16 are separate feature flags. In particular AVX512_FP16 denotes FP16 AVX-512 instructions and does not imply AMX_FP16 tile dot-product support. The v1-050 manual also states AMX FP16 support is Granite Rapids only (extract line 2353), so that statement must not be projected onto Sapphire Rapids. |
| AMX throughput, latency, alignment, tile dimensions | Optimization Manual v1-050 §§20.2.1–20.5.2, printed pp. 20-2–20-4; extract lines 26274–26340 | The manual gives a Sapphire Rapids AMX frequency-license discussion and a table of AMX instruction throughput/latency, recommends reducing repeated LDTILECFG/TILERELEASE pairs, calls for 64-byte data alignment, and describes 1024-byte tile limits and BF16 K width up to 32 elements. These are guidance values for the manual's stated target, not a substitute for measurement on the exact SKU and system. |
| AMX implementation examples/state | Optimization Manual v1-050 §§20.19–20.20, printed pp. 20-59–20-66; extract lines 28397–28573 | Includes intrinsics interface/example, compiler-generated AMX assembly showing tile configuration/release and save/restore around calls, plus XSTATE/XFD and OS enablement. The Linux/OS allocation caveat matters: CPUID alone does not ensure user code can execute AMX. |
| Linux dynamic XSTATE permission and AMX first use | Linux Kernel docs, [latest rendered page](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/arch/x86/xstate.html), local `linux-xstate/xstate-latest.html` lines 255–270; pinned kernel v6.12 source `linux-xstate/xstate-v6.12.rst` lines 58–81 | `ARCH_GET_XCOMP_PERM` reports features for which the userspace process has permission; `ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM` requests permission. The docs explicitly say permission is per process, inherited by `fork(2)`, and cleared by `exec(3)`. First use of a dynamically enabled instruction traps; if permitted, the handler allocates the larger XSTATE buffer for that task. Thus process permission and per-task first-use state-buffer allocation are separate. The docs also cover alternate signal stack sizing. |
| AMX emulation of higher-precision GEMM | Optimization Manual v1-050 §20.21, printed pp. 20-66–20-68; extract lines 28574 onward | Describes BF16 decomposition and AMX products for approximating higher precision. It warns about exponent range, denormals, accumulation order, and non-identical results; use it as algorithmic guidance, not a proof of any particular implementation's accuracy. |
| SIMD reduction / shuffle / rounding ideas | Optimization Manual v1-050 §§7.6.1, 15.11, 17.8, 17.10, 17.15.4, and 17.18; examples at printed pp. 7-11–7-12, 15-32–15-37, 17-31–17-36, 17-48, and 17-64; extract lines 11800–11890, 23055ff, 23220ff, 23682ff, 24238ff | Gives SSE horizontal-reduction examples (`movhlps`, `pshufd`, `haddps`, `dpps`), AVX2/AVX-512 shuffle and data movement advice, AVX-512 two-source permute examples, embedded RNE/SAE semantics, and vector-reduce examples. Chapter 17 also contains Skylake-specific implementation latency/port discussion; do not transfer those cycle counts to Sapphire Rapids. |
| Historical AVX2/AVX-512 frequency discussion | Optimization Manual v1-050 §2.6.3, printed pp. 2-29–2-31, extract lines 3432–3505 | This section explicitly concerns Skylake Server and gives Skylake-specific frequency licenses, thresholds, examples, and monitoring events (including a Xeon Platinum 8180 example). It is historical context only; do not use its frequencies, license boundaries, `-qopt-zmm-usage`, or measured ratios as a 8454H specification. |
| SIMD/AVX2/AVX-512/FP16 background | Optimization Manual v1-050 §§3.4, 5.3–5.4, 15, 17, and 18 | Read selectively for dependence/aliasing, data contiguity/alignment, intrinsic vs auto-vectorization, AVX/AVX2 programming, AVX-512 shuffle/reduction/rounding, and AVX-512 FP16. Chapter 18 is specifically AVX-512 FP16; it is not AMX FP16. The manual is broader than Sapphire Rapids and includes older microarchitecture-specific guidance. Consult current compiler output and measurements for code-generation claims. |

## Chapter 20 implementation-practice cross-check against ozAMX

The source references here are read-only observations from `src/gemm.cpp`; the repository may evolve independently of this snapshot. Manual locations use the extracted ORM text and printed pages.

| Manual advice / fact | Source location | Comparison with current implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Minimize tile loads by keeping K outside the M/N accumulator loops, preloading one side for reuse, and using a 2D accumulator arrangement. | ORM §20.5.5.1, printed pp. 20-10–20-12; extract lines 26520–26608. §20.5.5.3 demonstrates interleaved GEMM, pp. 20-13–20-14; lines 26609–26695. | The microkernel uses four C accumulator tiles for a 32×32 output microtile and an `ai`/`bi` schedule that avoids reloading the same A/B operand on adjacent products within each K slice (`src/gemm.cpp:252-278`). It reloads panels as it advances to other microtiles. FP64 product microkernels reload A and B for each product (`:280-296`). The source has no explicit load/TDP software pipeline or prefetch; compiler scheduling is a separate question. |
| Cache-block A/B/C working sets, using suitable M/N/K cache block sizes; K blocking can require extra accumulator traffic. | ORM §20.6, printed pp. 20-21–20-23; extract lines 26852–26997. | Source sets AMX work dimensions `BM=BN=BK=256`, `TM=TN=TK=32` (`src/gemm.cpp:21`), packs all matrix panels into global `Packed32`/`Packed64` arrays (`:153-160, 173-249`), then each output block loops across all `kblocks` (`:371-387, 456-480`). This is matrix/tile blocking, but no separate `MC_CACHE/N_CACHE/K_CACHE` cache-blocking loop or bounded cache-working-set buffer is visible. Any effect on the 8454H's caches is an inference; these source facts do not quantify the performance cost. |
| Consider non-temporal AMX tile loads (`TILELOADDT1`) when one large, low-reuse stream evicts a smaller, high-reuse stream from L1. | ORM §20.8–20.8.1, printed pp. 20-25–20-27; extract lines 26998–27090. | The compute paths issue `_tile_loadd` only (`src/gemm.cpp:264-270, 288-291`); no `_tile_stream_loadd`/TILELOADDT1 is present. Whether bypassing L1 would help the already packed A/B panels depends on actual reuse and cache behavior and needs measurement. |
| AMX/AVX-512 software interleaving may overlap work across different units; the manual uses double-buffered temporary C to pipeline a preceding layer's post-processing with the next iteration's AMX work. | ORM §20.11.2, printed pp. 20-32–20-34; extract lines 27266–27378. | Source exposes AMX TDP instructions and scalar C reconstruction, but no explicit AVX-512 post-processing pipeline or two-buffer temporary-C scheme (`src/gemm.cpp:252-296, 368-394, 453-487`). The public GEMM entry point completes one product before returning. This makes the manual's layer-pipeline optimization a possible future fused-path idea, not a claim that such a pipeline can be added without resource competition or accuracy/performance trade-offs. |
| AMX TDP can close the second AVX-512 FMA port (“port five”); opening/closing it around short AVX-512 regions may stall. Manual describes a 100–300-instruction case and a TILEZERO workaround in that context. | ORM §20.11.3, printed p. 20-35; extract lines 27379–27410. | There is no explicit AVX-512 block near the TDP source in this implementation. Compiler-generated vector instructions in library/loop code are not ruled out by source inspection; disassembly and profiling would be needed to establish interaction. The manual's stated percentage and instruction-count range are not a 8454H guarantee. |
| Reuse input/output buffers to reduce memory footprint and cache evictions; in a layer graph the manual describes ping-pong/reusable buffers. | ORM §20.12, printed pp. 20-37–20-38; extract lines 27462–27510. | This is a per-call standalone GEMM API with fresh vectors for split, pack, and result data (`src/gemm.cpp:334-356, 419-441`); no layer graph or reusable caller-provided scratch object is visible. Scratch lifetime reuse could reduce allocation/initialization overhead, but that is an inference and would need a separately designed API/measurement. |
| Flat BF16 matrices may be transposed/repacked to VNNI form using vector shuffles; the manual's Flat-to-VNNI example transforms 16×8 into 4×32 using ZMM registers and masks. | ORM §20.16.3, printed pp. 20-48–20-50; extract lines 27892–27985. | The packer does create a VNNI-like B layout: for each column it stores the two adjacent K BF16 values consecutively (`src/gemm.cpp:197-207`, index mapping at `:168-170`; same logic for FP64 at `:235-245`). The actual packing is scalar nested loops, not the manual's ZMM/mask transpose. This is a static implementation difference; its cost is not quantified here. |
| Choose thread partitioning around cache locality and bandwidth: M tends to preserve output/activation locality but all cores read B; N can lower B read bandwidth but may hurt next-layer locality; K splits inputs but needs partial C reduction. Affinity and avoiding multiple AMX workers per physical core are recommended. | ORM §§20.17–20.17.3.4, printed pp. 20-52–20-55; extract lines 28036–28155. | Current work is parallelized across independent `(mblock,nblock)` C blocks with `schedule(static)`; K is not split among threads (`src/gemm.cpp:357-388, 442-481`). The code makes no affinity binding request. Runtime affinity/SMT placement is therefore environment-dependent. The manual's observations are DL/layer locality guidance; for a standalone GEMM, actual best partitioning remains shape/cache/runtime dependent. |

### Allocation alignment observed in source

- `TileConfig` is explicitly `__attribute__((packed, aligned(64)))` (`src/gemm.cpp:128-140`).
- Packed A and B arrays are allocated by `new std::uint16_t[ma/nb]` and owned by `unique_ptr` (`src/gemm.cpp:153-160, 181-185, 221-224`). This guarantees suitable alignment for `uint16_t`, not a 64-byte cache-line alignment. No aligned allocator, over-aligned element type, `alignas(64)` storage wrapper, or runtime pointer-alignment assertion appears in those paths. Thus the source does not guarantee 64-byte base alignment; allocator-specific observed alignment is a separate dynamic fact. Panel strides happen to be multiples of 64 bytes, so an aligned base would keep panel starts aligned, but they cannot strengthen the base guarantee.
- `float block[BM*BN]`, `double block[BM*BN]`, and `float micro[TM*TN]` are ordinary automatic arrays without `alignas(64)` (`src/gemm.cpp:368-369, 453-454`). The source guarantees only each type's required alignment. The external A/B/C pointers are also not constrained to 64-byte alignment by `validate_layout` (`:304-314`).

### Scope boundary for performance conclusions

The paper's stated scratch/copy design and this source's global packed-panel allocations are distinct design choices: compute kernels take panel pointers directly from the shared packed arrays (`src/gemm.cpp:261-262, 286-287`) and issue tile loads from those addresses; no per-worker/per-block software copy into another local panel buffer is visible. This confirms the source difference only. It does not establish that the paper's local copy is faster, nor how much any design difference contributes to a measured gap. The manual's idealized resource overlap also should not be read as free simultaneous peak AMX and AVX-512 throughput: the same Chapter 20 documents a shared port/frequency interaction, and actual overlap must be measured on the target system.

## CPU applicability and limits

Intel's Optimization Manual v1-050 §2.2 explicitly associates Sapphire Rapids with Golden Cove cores, AMX, and AVX-512. For a Xeon Platinum 8454H, use its actual CPUID/XSTATE and OS state as the deciding capability check. AVX512_FP16, AVX512_BF16, AMX_BF16, AMX_INT8, and AMX_TILE are different features. **AVX512_FP16 does not imply AMX_FP16.** The v1-050 manual's statement that AMX FP16 is Granite Rapids only, plus the separate AMX_FP16 CPUID bit in SDM v093, makes it unsafe to infer AMX FP16 from AVX-512 FP16 support.

For Linux AMX enablement, distinguish two scopes: `ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM` grants permission per process (inherited across `fork`, cleared by `exec`); on each task's first AMX instruction, the kernel traps and allocates that task's larger XSTATE buffer. A `GET_XCOMP_PERM` result therefore reports process permission, not whether every worker task has already completed first-use allocation. A check performed in a separate process cannot establish that a worker thread in another, target process lacks permission. The current wrapper function is named `request_amx_permission_for_current_thread` (`src/runtime.cpp:22`), and its status strings say permission is available/granted “for this thread” (`:35,41`); those names are narrower than the documented process-level permission. They do not change the kernel's scope or guarantee that each task has already had its XSTATE buffer allocated.

The manuals are normative or optimization guidance at different scopes. The SDM instruction entries define architectural behavior. The Optimization Manual's Chapter 20 is targeted to Sapphire Rapids AMX and is useful for tile programming, state, and examples. Its Skylake Server AVX frequency chapter is explicitly not a 8454H tuning table. The Intrinsics Guide snapshot is version 3.6.9 from 2024; it is an intrinsic/latency/throughput lookup aid, while the v093 SDM is the newer authority for instruction semantics.

## Scope of reading

I read the relevant PDF front matter, contents, and cited sections/pages listed above, and cross-checked the BF16 convert and tile pseudocode in the current SDM. I did not read every page of the 895-page Optimization Manual or 600/771/782-page SDM volumes, did not download the full ten-volume SDM, and did not treat any one frequency or throughput table as a performance guarantee for the exact 8454H server configuration. Ghostscript page counts and text extracts were generated locally; ORM extraction has the CID-font caveat noted above.
